module_title: Setting Prices That Work for You and Buyers

lessons.title: Understanding market price vs. cost price
lessons.body:
As a farmer, you must know two numbers: your cost price and the market price. Cost price is what it costs you to produce one unitâsay, one bucket of tomatoes. Market price is what buyers are willing to pay on a given day. If you sell below cost, you lose money. If you price too high, you may not sell at all.

To calculate cost price, add up all your expenses for a season: seeds, fertilizer, labour, transport, and any bags or crates. Then divide by the number of units you harvested. For example, if you spent 200,000 shillings to grow 100 buckets of tomatoes, your cost price is 2,000 shillings per bucket. That is your break-even pointâthe lowest price you can accept without losing money.

Market price changes daily. It depends on supply (how many other farmers are selling), demand (how many buyers want your crop), and quality. Visit your local market or call a trader to ask today's price. If the market price is 3,000 shillings per bucket, you make a profit of 1,000 shillings per bucket. If it is 1,800 shillings, you would lose 200 shillings per bucketâso you might decide to hold your produce, sell in a different market, or process it into something else.

Never guess. Write down your cost price and check market prices regularly. A simple notebook or a phone note works. Knowing both numbers gives you power to negotiate and avoid selling at a loss.

lessons.title: How to negotiate a fair price with traders
lessons.body:
Negotiation is not a fight; it is a conversation to find a price that works for both you and the trader. Before you meet a trader, know your cost price and the current market price. Decide on your minimum priceâthe lowest you will acceptâand stick to it. If a trader offers less, you can politely say no and walk away.

Start by asking the trader for their price first. This gives you information. If their offer is below your minimum, do not get angry. Instead, explain the quality of your produce: âThese tomatoes are fresh, uniform, and well-packed. They will last longer on your shelf.â Use facts, not emotions. You can also mention that you have other buyers interested, but only if it is true.

If the trader's offer is close to your target, you can counter with a slightly higher price. For example, if they offer 2,500 shillings per bucket and your minimum is 2,800, you might say, âI can do 3,000 if you buy ten buckets.â This gives them a reason to agree. Sometimes traders will ask for a discount for bulk. That is fine if it still covers your costs and gives a small profit.

Remember, negotiation is about building a relationship. A trader who feels respected may come back next season and pay better. Do not burn bridges. But also do not sell below your minimum just to make a sale. Practice your negotiation with a friend before going to market. The more you do it, the easier it becomes.

lessons.title: Pricing by unit: bucket, bag, or kilo
lessons.body:
In many African markets, produce is sold by volume (bucket, bag) or by weight (kilo). Each unit has a different price, and you must know how to convert between them to compare offers. For example, a trader might offer 10,000 shillings per bag of maize, while another offers 500 shillings per kilo. Which is better? It depends on how many kilos are in a bag.

Start by standardising your units. Use a consistent containerâlike a 20-litre bucket or a 50-kg bag. Weigh or measure one unit to know exactly how much produce it holds. For instance, if your bucket holds 12 kilos of tomatoes, and you sell at 2,500 shillings per bucket, that is about 208 shillings per kilo. If a trader offers 250 shillings per kilo, that is better. But if they offer 180 shillings per kilo, it is worse.

Also consider the cost of packaging. A bag costs money, and a bucket may be reusable. If you sell by kilo, you need a scale, which may not be available in rural markets. Many buyers prefer buckets because they can see the volume. But selling by kilo can be more accurate and often fetches a higher price per unit.

When negotiating, always ask the trader to specify the unit: âIs that price per bucket or per kilo?â If they say per bag, ask how many kilos are in the bag. Then do the math. Keep a small notebook with conversions for your common crops. This prevents you from being cheated. For example, if a bag of maize is 50 kilos, and the price is 30,000 shillings per bag, that is 600 shillings per kilo. If another trader offers 650 shillings per kilo, you know the second is better.

Knowing your units gives you confidence and helps you compare prices across different markets and traders.

lessons.title: When to offer discounts and when to hold firm
lessons.body:
Discounts can help you sell faster, especially when you have a perishable crop or a large harvest. But offering a discount too often can train buyers to expect lower prices and eat into your profits. The key is to discount strategically, not desperately.

Offer a discount when: you have a surplus that will spoil if not sold quickly; a buyer purchases a large quantity (bulk discount); or you want to build a relationship with a new trader who might become a regular customer. For example, if you have 50 buckets of tomatoes and only two days before they spoil, you might offer a 10% discount for anyone who buys five buckets or more. That is 2,500 shillings per bucket instead of 2,800. You still cover your cost and avoid total loss.

Hold firm when: your produce is high quality and in demand; you have storage or can process the crop; or the buyer is trying to lowball you below your minimum price. If a trader offers 1,500 shillings per bucket when your cost is 2,000, do not accept. Politely explain that you cannot go below your cost. If they insist, let them walk away. Another buyer may come.

A useful rule: never discount below your cost price. Your cost price is your floor. If you must sell below cost to avoid total loss, do it only as a last resort, and calculate the loss so you can plan better next season.

Also, consider non-cash discounts: free delivery, extra produce, or flexible payment terms. These can satisfy a buyer without lowering your headline price. For example, âI cannot reduce the price, but I can deliver to your shop for free.â That saves the buyer transport money and keeps your price intact.

Always write down the discount you gave and why. Review it later to see if it helped or hurt your business.

lessons.title: Checking prices at different local markets
lessons.body:
Prices for the same crop can vary widely from one market to another, even within a few kilometres. A bucket of tomatoes might sell for 2,000 shillings in your village market but 3,500 shillings in the nearest town. Checking prices at different markets helps you find the best buyer and avoid being underpaid.

How to check prices: visit at least three markets in your area on different days. Talk to traders, other farmers, and market officials. Ask: âWhat is the price per bucket today?â Write down the prices, the date, and the market name. Also note the quality of produce being sold at that priceâyours might be better or worse. If you cannot travel, use your phone. Call a friend or fellow farmer in another market. Some countries have SMS or WhatsApp groups where farmers share daily prices. Join them.

Once you have prices from several markets, compare them to your cost price and transport costs. If Market A offers 3,000 shillings per bucket but it costs 500 shillings per bucket to transport there, your net is 2,500. If Market B offers 2,800 and transport is only 100, your net is 2,700. So Market B is better even though the headline price is lower. Always calculate net price after transport.

Also consider market fees, loading charges, and your time. A market that is far may not be worth it if the extra price is small. But if the price difference is large, it can be worth the trip. For example, if you have 20 buckets and the price difference is 500 shillings per bucket, that is an extra 10,000 shillingsâenough to pay for transport and still profit.

Keep a simple record of prices over time. You will start to see patterns: prices may be higher during festivals or when supply is low. Use that knowledge to plan your planting and selling.

lessons.title: Setting a minimum price and sticking to it
lessons.body:
A minimum price is the lowest amount you are willing to accept for your produce. It protects you from selling at a loss and from being pressured by aggressive traders. Setting it is easy; sticking to it requires discipline.

To set your minimum price, start with your cost price. Add a small profit marginâeven 10% is better than nothing. For example, if your cost is 2,000 shillings per bucket, your minimum could be 2,200 shillings. This covers your costs and gives a little profit. If the market price is higher, you can ask for more, but never go below your minimum.

Write your minimum price on a piece of paper or in your phone. Before you go to market, remind yourself: âI will not sell below 2,200 shillings per bucket.â When a trader offers less, politely say, âI cannot go below 2,200. That is my minimum.â If they refuse, thank them and move on. There will be other buyers.

It is tempting to break your minimum when you see your produce starting to spoil or when you need cash urgently. To avoid this, plan ahead. Harvest only what you can sell in a reasonable time. If you have a perishable crop, consider processing it (e.g., drying tomatoes) or selling to a different market where prices are higher. Also, build a small emergency fund so you are not forced to sell at a loss.

Sticking to your minimum builds your reputation as a serious farmer who knows their business. Traders will learn that they cannot cheat you. Over time, they may even offer you better prices because they respect your firmness. Remember, your minimum price is your bottom lineâyour business depends on it.

quiz.q: What is the cost price of a product?
options: A) The price at which you sell to traders
B) The total expenses divided by the number of units produced
C) The highest price in the market
D) The price after adding profit
quiz.explanation: Cost price is calculated by dividing total production expenses by the number of units harvested.

quiz.q: If you spent 300,000 shillings to produce 150 buckets of tomatoes, what is your cost price per bucket?
quiz.explanation: 300,000 divided by 150 equals 2,000 shillings per bucket.

quiz.q: Why is it important to know the market price before selling?
options: A) To impress traders with your knowledge
B) To decide whether to sell, hold, or find another market
C) To set a price higher than everyone else
D) To avoid paying market fees
quiz.explanation: Knowing the market price helps you make informed decisions about selling or holding your produce.

quiz.q: What should you do if the market price is below your cost price?
options: A) Sell immediately to avoid loss
B) Hold your produce, find another market, or process it
C) Accept the price and learn from it
D) Borrow money to cover costs
quiz.explanation: Selling below cost means a loss, so you should explore alternatives like holding or processing.

quiz.q: During negotiation, why is it good to let the trader mention their price first?
options: B) It gives you information to counter-offer
D) It guarantees a higher price
quiz.explanation: Knowing the trader's offer helps you decide how to respond and whether it meets your minimum.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy if a trader offers a price below your minimum?
options: A) Accept it to maintain the relationship
B) Politely decline and explain your minimum
quiz.explanation: Politely declining and stating your minimum keeps the relationship respectful and protects your profit.

quiz.q: Why might offering a bulk discount be beneficial?
options: A) It always increases total profit
B) It encourages larger purchases and reduces spoilage
C) It makes you look generous
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Bulk discounts can move larger volumes quickly, reducing the risk of spoilage and covering costs.

quiz.q: What is a non-cash discount you can offer instead of lowering price?
options: C) A promise to buy from them later
quiz.explanation: Free delivery is a non-cash incentive that saves the buyer money without reducing your price.

quiz.q: If a bucket holds 12 kilos of tomatoes and you sell at 2,400 shillings per bucket, what is the price per kilo?
quiz.explanation: 2,400 divided by 12 equals 200 shillings per kilo.

quiz.q: Why is it important to standardise your units when selling?
options: B) To compare prices accurately across different offers
quiz.explanation: Standard units allow you to calculate and compare prices per kilo or per bucket consistently.

quiz.q: What should you consider when comparing prices at different markets?
options: B) Transport costs, market fees, and net price
quiz.explanation: Net price after all costs determines the true benefit of selling in a particular market.

quiz.q: How can you check prices at other markets without traveling?
options: A) Guess based on past prices
B) Call a friend or use farmer WhatsApp groups
C) Ask the first trader you meet
quiz.explanation: Phone calls and social media groups are effective ways to get current market prices from afar.

quiz.q: What is a minimum price?
options: A) The price you hope to get
B) The lowest price you will accept for your produce
quiz.explanation: Minimum price is your bottom line, below which you will not sell to avoid loss.

quiz.q: How should you set your minimum price?
options: A) By matching your neighbour's price
B) By adding a profit margin to your cost price
C) By asking a trader to decide
D) By using last year's price
quiz.explanation: Your minimum should cover cost price plus a small profit to ensure sustainability.

quiz.q: What can help you stick to your minimum price when you need cash urgently?
quiz.explanation: An emergency fund reduces pressure to sell below your minimum price.

quiz.q: What is the risk of always offering discounts?
options: A) Buyers may expect lower prices and your profits shrink
B) You will sell too fast
quiz.explanation: Frequent discounts can condition buyers to always ask for less, eroding your profit margins.

quiz.q: If a trader offers 500 shillings per kilo and a bag contains 50 kilos, what is the price per bag?
quiz.explanation: 500 shillings per kilo times 50 kilos equals 25,000 shillings per bag.

quiz.q: What is a fair negotiation tactic?
options: A) Threatening to walk away immediately
B) Explaining the quality and value of your produce
quiz.explanation: Highlighting quality and value justifies your price and encourages a fair offer.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records of prices from different markets?
options: A) To show off to other farmers
B) To identify patterns and plan future sales
C) To report to the government
quiz.explanation: Records help you understand seasonal trends and make better marketing decisions.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of selling by kilo instead of by bucket?
options: B) It can be more accurate and fetch a higher price per unit
quiz.explanation: Selling by weight is precise and often allows you to charge more per unit of produce.

quiz.q: If your cost price is 1,800 shillings per bucket and you want a 20% profit, what is your minimum price?
quiz.explanation: 20% of 1,800 is 360, so minimum price is 1,800 + 360 = 2,160 shillings.

quiz.q: What should you do if a trader insists on a price below your cost?
options: B) Politely refuse and seek another buyer
quiz.explanation: Selling below cost leads to loss, so it's better to find a buyer who meets your minimum.

quiz.q: How can you build a reputation as a serious farmer?
options: B) By sticking to your minimum price
C) By selling to the first buyer
quiz.explanation: Firmly sticking to your minimum shows traders you are business-minded and not easily exploited.

quiz.q: What is a potential downside of traveling to a distant market for a higher price?
options: B) Transport costs may reduce your net profit
C) The market may be closed
D) You will pay more taxes
quiz.explanation: Higher transport costs can offset the higher market price, so calculate net profit.

quiz.q: Why is it important to write down your cost price and minimum price?
options: B) To remember and stick to them during negotiation
C) To apply for a loan
quiz.explanation: Writing down these figures helps you stay disciplined and avoid emotional selling.

quiz.q: What is a good way to practice negotiation?
quiz.explanation: Role-playing builds confidence and helps you anticipate trader responses.

quiz.q: If a trader offers 2,500 shillings per bucket and your minimum is 2,800, what could you propose?
options: B) Ask for 3,000 if they buy ten buckets
quiz.explanation: Counter-offering with a bulk condition can bridge the gap and meet your minimum.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a discount?
options: B) To increase sales volume or reduce spoilage
quiz.explanation: Discounts are a tool to move produce faster, especially when perishable or in surplus.

quiz.q: How can you calculate the price per kilo if you sell a 50-kg bag for 40,000 shillings?
quiz.explanation: 40,000 divided by 50 equals 800 shillings per kilo.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot sell your perishable produce at your minimum price?
options: B) Process it or sell below cost as a last resort
quiz.explanation: Processing or a last-resort sale can recover some value and prevent total loss.
